meta.rule: Every non-null value was read on a fetched page/PDF/dataset. Derived values are flagged in 'note'. Null = could not verify.
meta.fetch_caveats: ipcc.ch, unep.org, un.org and nature.com returned HTTP 403/redirects to the fetcher; IPCC/UNEP/Nature content was read from official-copy mirrors or reputable secondary coverage named in each 'source'.

global.label: Global warming by 2100 under current policies (UNEP)
global.source: UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2026 'The point of return' (21 Oct 2026), as reported by Carbon Brief; unep.org blocked automated fetch
global.note: 2.8°C given 'with a 66% chance'; Carbon Brief adds a 10% chance warming exceeds 3.4°C. Same report: unconditional NDCs 2.7°C, all NDCs 2.6°C, NDCs + net-zero pledges 2.1°C (all 66%). Report-page: https://unep.org/en/publications/report/emissions-gap-report-2026

global.label: Global warming by 2100 under current policies (Climate Action Tracker)
global.source: Climate Action Tracker, Warming Projections Global Update, 12 Nov 2026 (COP31)
global.note: Median moved from 2.64°C to 2.72°C. Range = Figure 2 'Policies & action with range' High +2.9°C / Low +2.5°C (policy-emissions range). The thermometer graphic also prints +3.4°C and +2.2°C near this bar, but extracted text does not say what they denote. Other CAT scenarios: 2030 & 2035 targets 2.6°C; pledges & targets 2.1°C; optimistic 1.9°C. Temperatures keep rising after 2100.

tipping_points.label: Greenland ice sheet collapse (GrIS)
tipping_points.consequence: Multi-metre sea-level rise over millennia; +0.13°C global and +0.5–3°C regional warming feedback
tipping_points.source: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022, Science 377, Table 1; GTPR 2025 Summary
tipping_points.note: Read from article PDF copy: https://krichlab.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Science-Armstrong-Mckay-2022-Exceeding-1.5-oC-global-warming-could-trigger-multiple-climate-tipping-points.pdf. GTPR 2025: likely tipping point around 1.5°C; ice sheets at risk since at least 1°C. Metre figure (e.g. ~7 m) not stated in text read, so not given.

tipping_points.label: West Antarctic ice sheet collapse (WAIS)
tipping_points.consequence: Multi-metre sea-level rise; +0.05°C global, +1.0°C regional feedback
tipping_points.source: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022, Science 377, Table 1; GTPR 2025 Summary
tipping_points.note: GTPR 2025: likely tipping point around 1.5°C; parts of polar ice sheets may already have crossed tipping points.

tipping_points.label: Low-latitude (warm-water) coral reef die-off (REEF)
tipping_points.consequence: Reef ecosystem collapse; reefs support up to a billion people and almost a million species
tipping_points.source: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022, Science 377, Table 1; GTPR 2025 Summary (case study)
tipping_points.note: GTPR 2025 revised the threshold DOWN to 1.2°C central (range 1–1.5°C) and judged it already crossed; see gtpr2025_coral_headline.

tipping_points.label: Boreal permafrost abrupt thaw (PFAT)
tipping_points.consequence: Abrupt thaw adds ~50% to gradual permafrost carbon emissions (~0.04°C per °C of warming by 2100)
tipping_points.source: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022, Science 377, Table 1
tipping_points.note: Full boreal permafrost collapse (PFTP, separate element): 4.0°C (3.0–6.0), ~50 yr (10–300), 125–250 GtC / 175–350 GtCe. GTPR 2025: land permafrost likely tips around 1.5°C.

tipping_points.label: Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation collapse (AMOC)
tipping_points.consequence: −0.5°C global, −4 to −10°C regional (N. Atlantic) cooling; threatens food/water security, severe NW-Europe winters
tipping_points.source: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022, Science 377, Table 1; GTPR 2025 Summary
tipping_points.note: GTPR 2025: AMOC 'likely' has a tipping point around 2.0°C and is at risk of collapse below 2°C; tipping cannot be ruled out at current warming.

tipping_points.label: Amazon rainforest dieback (AMAZ)
tipping_points.consequence: Partial: 30 GtC / +0.1°C; total: 75 GtC / +0.2°C global; +0.4–2.0°C regional; disrupted S. American rainfall
tipping_points.source: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022, Science 377, Table 1; GTPR 2025 Summary
tipping_points.note: 2022 threshold is for climate alone. GTPR 2025: climate change plus deforestation put widespread dieback at risk below 2°C; regime shifts in the 1.5–2°C range; >100 million people depend on the forest.

tipping_points.label: Labrador-Irminger Seas / subpolar gyre convection collapse (LABC)
tipping_points.consequence: −0.5°C global, −3°C regional cooling around the North Atlantic; disrupted European/N. American weather
tipping_points.source: Armstrong McKay et al. 2022, Science 377, Table 1; GTPR 2025 Summary
tipping_points.note: GTPR 2025: sub-polar gyre likely tips around 1.5°C.

tipping_points.label: GTPR 2025 headline: warm-water coral reefs have passed their tipping point
tipping_points.consequence: Regional tipping likely underway; >99% chance of tipping even if warming stabilises at 1.5°C; first Earth-system tipping point judged crossed
tipping_points.source: Global Tipping Points Report 2025 Summary (Univ. of Exeter, 13 Oct 2025); range from National Oceanography Centre release
tipping_points.note: Answer: YES. Range 1–1.5°C quoted in https://www.noc.ac.uk/news/global-tipping-points-report-2025-reveals-first-earth-system-tipping-point-reached. Report says warming must go back below 1.2°C, then 1°C, to keep functional reefs at scale.

consequences.label: Share of people outside the human climate niche at ~2.7°C (2080–2100)
consequences.source: Lenton et al. 2023, Nature Sustainability 6, abstract
consequences.note: Abstract says 'one-third (22–39%)'; 33 = one-third. Main text: 29% (2.8 bn) from temperature only, 39% (3.7 bn) with demographic change; at 1.5°C 14% and 28%. Read from copy: https://edepot.wur.nl/632994

consequences.label: People exposed to unprecedented heat (mean annual temp ≥29°C) at ~2.7°C
consequences.note: Drops to 5% (0.4 billion) at 1.5°C, about a 5-fold fall. The paper's warming span for current policies: 2.7 (2.0–3.6)°C.

consequences.label: People already outside the human climate niche (today)
consequences.scenario: Present-day climate (paper cites present warming of ~1.2°C)
consequences.source: Lenton et al. 2023, Nature Sustainability 6, abstract
consequences.note: Exeter press release adds ~60 million already exposed to dangerous heat (https://news.exeter.ac.uk/research/limiting-global-warming-to-1-5c-would-save-billions-from-dangerously-hot-climate).

consequences.label: India: people exposed to unprecedented heat at 2.7°C
consequences.note: Largest of any country; ~90 million at 1.5°C.

consequences.label: Nigeria: people exposed to unprecedented heat at 2.7°C
consequences.note: Second largest; <40 million at 1.5°C. Next: Indonesia ~100 M, Philippines and Pakistan >80 M each, then Sudan, Niger. Burkina Faso and Mali near 100% of land exposed; Brazil has the largest exposed land area.

consequences.label: Global yield change per +1°C of global warming (wheat / rice / maize / soybean)
consequences.unit: % per °C (value = wheat; range spans the four crops)
consequences.scenario: No CO2 fertilisation, effective adaptation or genetic improvement
consequences.source: Zhao et al. 2017, PNAS 114(35), abstract (via Europe PMC PMC5584412)
consequences.note: Wheat −6.0%, rice −3.2%, maize −7.4%, soybean −3.1% per °C; these crops supply about two-thirds of human calories. Not an IPCC AR6 number: WG2 SPM could not be fetched.

consequences.label: Glacier mass remaining if warming stabilises at 2.7°C (vs 1.5°C)
consequences.source: Zekollari et al. 2025, as cited in CAT Global Update Nov 2026, section 3.1
consequences.note: Secondary citation (read in CAT), not checked in the original paper.

consequences.label: Committed sea-level rise over 2000 years by peak warming
consequences.source: IPCC AR6 WG1 SPM section B.5 and Chapter 9 Executive Summary
consequences.note: 2–3 m at 1.5°C; 2–6 m at 2°C; 4–10 m at 3°C; 12–16 m at 4°C; 19–22 m at 5°C (low confidence / medium agreement, limited evidence).

consequences.label: Tide gauges where former 1-in-100-yr extreme sea levels occur yearly by 2100
consequences.source: IPCC AR6 WG1 Chapter 9 Executive Summary (ITLOS-hosted excerpt)
consequences.note: 19–31% of gauges by 2050. Overall such extremes 160–530 times more frequent by 2100 (medium confidence).
